meta.title: Zulu A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Zulu → English (see the Zulu, recall the meaning) and English → Zulu (see an English meaning, recall the Zulu). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to manage simple, routine exchanges of information on familiar matters — personal and family information, shopping, the local area, work — and to describe in simple terms their background, their surroundings and what they immediately need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Zulu, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 117 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — the months and the seasons, the points of the compass, languages and peoples, clothes, work and jobs, relatives and neighbours, feelings, travel and the address, the weather and the countryside, the body and health, more food and the kitchen, the things of a home, talking and telling, telling when, plans and problems, and the everyday verbs of doing — and the other 633 are the commonest remaining words of the Zulu Wikipedia, counted by the WHOLE word: Zulu joins its prefixes to the word (abantu, kumuntu, ngiyahamba), so every form of a noun or a verb is added together. That corpus is encyclopaedic, which shows in the fill (history, government, sport). The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words met most often come first. Only words English Wiktionary has an entry for can be taught here, and a few everyday words are missing from it (kodwa 'but', namuhla 'today', nini 'when'). A noun is shown whole with its NOUN CLASS — the prefix family that every adjective, verb and pronoun agreeing with it echoes; the Zulu Noun Classes deck, first in this collection, teaches them — and its plural and locative ('at, in, to'): 446 nouns here. A verb, an adjective or a relative is shown by its stem with a hyphen (-hamba, -khulu), as Zulu dictionaries print it, since none stands without a prefix; the 283 verbs give their infinitive and plural command, and behind the Tenses fold their present, negative, past and future by person, taken from Wiktionary's own tables. Beneath each headword is Wiktionary's tone-marked spelling (umúntu, -hámba): ordinary Zulu writing marks no tone, but the language has it. Example sentences are few: 23 of the 750 words have one, from Wiktionary's usage examples and from Tatoeba, which holds about a hundred Zulu sentences; none is invented. A speaker reads the word and each sentence where the device has a Zulu voice. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, noun classes, forms, tables and tones: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Zulu Wikipedia, articles of the 2026-11-01 dump (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: English Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
